claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 begins in a uniform high-temperature BCC state with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
An intermediate isothermal hold during cooling permits sufficient atomic diffusion to occur.
Diffusion during the intermediate hold produces local compositional fluctuations or microsegregation.
Local compositional fluctuations modify the local free-energy landscape and reduce the nucleation barrier for secondary phases.
Reduced secondary-phase nucleation barriers lead to a multiphase microstructure.
A hold near 800 degrees Celsius for 2–3 hours falls within the diffusion-active kinetic window required by the proposed mechanism.
The controlled comparison consists of an approximately 800 degrees Celsius, 2–3 hour intermediate hold versus rapid quenching from the same high-temperature BCC state.
Rapid quenching minimizes diffusion and local compositional variation.
The rapidly quenched baseline will predominantly retain a metastable, comparatively homogeneous BCC microstructure.
Samples receiving the intermediate hold will contain more discernible secondary phases and greater microstructural heterogeneity than rapidly quenched samples.
Secondary phases will occur preferentially in regions showing local elemental enrichment or depletion.
Possible secondary phases include FCC, B2, or other intermetallic phases.
The mechanism applies only in a temperature-time regime where diffusion is activated but bulk equilibrium transformation is not completed.
The mechanism should not operate when cooling is sufficiently rapid or temperature sufficiently low that diffusion is negligible.
At excessively high temperatures or after excessively long holds, full-equilibrium phase formation may supersede the proposed fluctuation-assisted nucleation behavior.
The magnitude and spatial scale of compositional fluctuations depend on hold temperature, hold duration, and diffusion kinetics.
Thermal-history variations can alter phase content and grain morphology in compositionally complex alloys.

A lack of statistically significant compositional or phase-distribution differences, or a lack of spatial association between partitioning and secondary phases, would falsify the proposed mechanism under the tested conditions.
